lessonRef.unitTitle: Mathematical Habits and Place Value to One Million
lessonRef.focus: making sense of large numbers and unfamiliar problems
lessonRef.title: Launch and diagnostic: making sense of large numbers and unfamiliar problems

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Read the example first. You are not expected to know this yet.

items.prompt: You are not sure whether a word problem wants you to add or multiply. What should you do first?

steps: Reread the problem and picture the situation.
Decide whether equal groups or a running total is being described.
workedSolution.answer: Reread the problem, picture the situation, and decide whether it describes equal groups (multiply) or a running total (add).

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Try each one. If you get stuck, write what you do know and move on.

items.prompt: A problem could be solved more than one way. What should you do before picking a method?
choices: Skip the problem without trying it.
Guess an answer and move on to the next problem.
Multiply every number in the problem together.
Think about which method fits the numbers best, then explain why you chose it.

items.prompt: You read a word problem with several numbers in it and are not sure where to start. What should you do first?
choices: Skip the problem without trying it.
Restate the problem in your own words and identify exactly what question is being asked.
Multiply every number in the problem together.
Guess an answer and move on to the next problem.

items.prompt: You solved a multi-digit problem, but the answer has way more digits than makes sense. What should you do?
choices: Skip the problem without trying it.
Multiply every number in the problem together.
Estimate the answer first, then compare your exact answer to the estimate to check for a place-value mistake.
Guess an answer and move on to the next problem.

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Show what you can do so far. This sets the starting point, not a grade.
